newsitem.title: USA: IBM seen hit by currency.
newsitem.headline: IBM seen hit by currency.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. reports first-quarter earnings Wednesday and, like many multinational companies, the computer giant is expected to be hurt by the stronger dollar outside the United States.

IBM will again report earnings after the stock market closes, a routine it adopted last quarter, to avoid some of the volatility in its stock during its meeting and conference call with analysts, which now begins at 4:30 p.m. EDT.
The consensus Wall Street analyst forecast for IBM is $2.28 a share, with estimates ranging from $2.10 to $2.37, according to the First Call service.
"They will have a big currency hit and they will probably talk about currency hitting the second quarter," said Gary Helmig, a SoundView Financial analyst.
So far, multinational companies like Digital Equipment Corp., Xerox Corp. and other corporations with large overseas operations have reported that the stronger dollar has hurt earnings.
When the exchange rates of the dollar vs. foreign currencies climb, revenues earned in those currencies are worth less when they are translated back to the United States.
For IBM, currency may hurt earnings by about 20 cents a share, analysts said.

The experts said a product transition in mainframes may also hurt mainframe sales, which may see a greater than normal decline, as some customers have held off buying as they anticipate a new mainframe upgrade, due possibly in June.

"I assumed mainframes were relatively weak," said Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst. He said he is looking for the bright spots in the quarter to be in the personal computer business and in computer services.
In the fourth quarter, IBM's services revenues surged 22 percent, compared with its overall revenue growth of 6 percent, including the negative impact from currency.

"They will talk about services growth," predicted Helmig. He said IBM will also likely report strength in North America, weakness in Europe and very strong growth in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly in Japan.

A few weeks ago, a rumour surfaced on Wall Street that IBM would pre-announce that it would not meet analysts' estimates for the first quarter. IBM said it does not comment on analysts' forecasts and many analysts discounted the rumour.
But within the range of analysts' estimates, there are some who believe IBM may come in below consensus, such as Daniel Mandresh at Merrill Lynch, who has an estimate of $2.10.
John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst, on the other hand, believes IBM will exceed Wall Street estimates, and that they will top the consensus estimate of $2.28 a share.

"I'm still hanging in there," Jones said Tuesday, when asked if he is still on track with his estimate of $2.35 a share and his somewhat contrarian position. Jones said that while he agrees that the mainframe business is very weak, it is only about 5 percent to 6 percent of total revenues.
He sees additional strength coming from IBM's storage and its original equipment manufacturing businesses.

Last year, IBM reported first-quarter net income of $1.4 billion, or $2.48 a share, excluding charges associated with software acquisitions and other items. Including the charges, profits were $774 million, or $1.41 a share.
IBM rose $2.625 to $140 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
